title: Primary Function of the Support Arm
learningObjectives: Identify the primary structural role of the support arm.
student: What is the primary structural function of the hollow rectangular support arm?
instructor: The arm carries the seat and occupant load and transfers that load to the machine frame.

title: Principal External Load
learningObjectives: Identify and idealize the dominant applied load.
student: Where is the principal external load applied, and how should it be idealized?
instructor: The seat and occupant load is represented by a concentrated vertical force P acting downward through the seat-post centerline.

title: Machine-Frame Support Condition
learningObjectives: Describe the fixed-support idealization and its reactions.
student: How should the machine-frame attachment at A be idealized?
instructor: Idealize A as a fixed support that prevents horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation. It can therefore supply horizontal and vertical reaction forces and a reaction moment.

title: Dominant Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the occupant load to the supporting machine frame.
student: Trace the dominant load path from the occupant to the machine frame.
instructor: Occupant → seat → seat post and mounting bracket → cantilever tube arm → fixed attachment at A → machine frame.

title: Why Evaluate Section a-a?
learningObjectives: Explain why the designated section carries bending demand.
student: Why is section a-a an appropriate location for a bending-stress evaluation?
instructor: Section a-a lies in the load path and carries the bending moment produced by the offset load. In a tip-loaded cantilever, the bending-moment magnitude increases toward the fixed support.

title: Governing Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Recognize the expected flexural normal-stress distribution.
student: What mechanical response is the focus of this problem, and what stress distribution should be expected through the tube depth?
instructor: Flexural normal stress is the focus. For elastic bending, normal stress varies linearly through the depth, is zero at the neutral axis, and reaches its largest tensile and compressive magnitudes at the outer fibers.

title: Geometry Governing Bending Resistance
learningObjectives: Relate hollow-section dimensions to bending resistance.
student: Which cross-sectional dimensions most strongly affect bending stress at section a-a?
instructor: The outer height H, outer width B, inner height h, and inner width b determine the second moment of area. Section height is especially influential because the rectangular inertia expression contains a cubic height term.

title: Student-Generated Cantilever Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the seat assembly into a mechanics model.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the cantilever model before consulting the instructor reference figure.
commonMistakes: Common omissions are the fixed-end moment, the distance from the load line to section a-a, or the inner tube dimensions.
student: Before using the instructor reference figure, replace the seat assembly with a cantilever-beam model. Show fixed support A, downward load P, distance x from the load line to section a-a, and the hollow rectangular section dimensions.
instructor: A valid model shows a horizontal cantilever fixed at the machine frame, a downward point load P through the seat-post centerline, section a-a located x from that load line, and concentric outer dimensions B by H with inner dimensions b by h.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the beam-bending model.
student: State the assumptions used in the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Assume static loading, a straight prismatic arm, a concentrated load P, linear-elastic material response, small deformation, plane sections, and concentric inner and outer rectangles. Neglect arm and hardware self-weight unless included in P, connection flexibility, local attachment effects, stress concentrations, fatigue, impact, and dynamics.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Sequence the equilibrium, section-property, and stress calculations.
student: List the mechanics calculation sequence before substituting numerical values.
instructor: Cut the arm at section a-a and determine internal shear and bending moment; calculate net area and locate the centroidal neutral axis; calculate the second moment of area; set c = H/2; apply |σmax| = |M|c/I; and identify the tensile and compressive extreme fibers.

title: Boundary Condition and Reactions at A
learningObjectives: Identify all reaction resultants admitted at the fixed support.
student: State the boundary condition at A and list the associated reaction resultants.
instructor: A is fixed and can provide horizontal reaction Ax, vertical reaction Ay, and reaction moment MA. For the assigned vertical load, Ay and MA are the nonzero reactions.

title: Internal Shear and Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Use section equilibrium to determine internal resultants.
commonMistakes: Do not use the full distance to fixed support A when the requested cut is section a-a; use the assigned distance x from the load line to the cut.
student: Cut the arm at section a-a and determine the internal shear force V and bending moment M. State your sign convention.
instructor: From equilibrium of the free-end segment, |V| = P = {{seat_V_lb}} lb and |M| = Px = {{seat_M_lbin}} lb·in. Under the common sagging-positive convention, this loading produces a negative or hogging bending moment at the cut.

title: Net Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the material area of a hollow rectangular tube.
student: Determine the net cross-sectional area of the hollow rectangular tube.
instructor: A = BH - bh = {{seat_area_in2}} in2.

title: Centroidal Neutral Axis
learningObjectives: Locate the neutral axis using section symmetry.
student: Locate the centroidal neutral axis for bending about the horizontal centroidal axis.
instructor: Because the outer and inner rectangles are concentric and symmetric, the centroid and horizontal neutral axis lie at the section center, halfway through the outer height.

title: Second Moment of Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the second moment of area about the bending axis.
commonMistakes: Use the outer width with the outer height and the inner width with the inner height. The height dimension is cubed.
student: Determine the second moment of area I of section a-a about its horizontal centroidal axis.
instructor: I = (BH3 - bh3)/12 = {{seat_I_in4}} in4.

title: Extreme-Fiber Distance and Section Modulus
learningObjectives: Determine extreme-fiber distance and elastic section modulus.
student: Determine the extreme-fiber distance c and the elastic section modulus S = I/c.
instructor: c = H/2 = {{seat_c_in}} in. Therefore S = I/c = {{seat_S_in3}} in3.

title: Maximum Normal Bending Stress
learningObjectives: Apply the flexure formula with consistent units.
commonMistakes: Use the moment at section a-a, not simply the force. Keep lb, in, and in4 units consistent.
student: Determine the maximum normal bending-stress magnitude at section a-a.
instructor: |σmax| = |M|c/I = {{seat_sigma_max_psi}} psi = {{seat_sigma_max_ksi}} ksi.

title: Tension and Compression Fibers
learningObjectives: Relate bending-moment sense to tensile and compressive stress locations.
student: For the downward seat load, identify the extreme fiber in tension and the extreme fiber in compression. State the bending sign convention used.
instructor: Using sagging moment as positive, the section moment is negative or hogging. The {{seat_tension_fiber}} is in tension and the {{seat_compression_fiber}} is in compression. Their stress magnitudes are equal because the section is symmetric about the neutral axis.

title: Sensitivity to Geometry and Offset
learningObjectives: Compare how geometry and load offset affect bending stress.
student: Which change would most effectively reduce bending stress: increasing outer height H, increasing outer width B, or reducing offset x? Explain the governing trends.
instructor: Increasing section height is generally very effective because the rectangular inertia contains a cubic height term, although the inner dimensions and packaging constraints also matter. Reducing x lowers moment and stress linearly. Increasing B generally increases inertia approximately linearly when the remaining geometry is held comparable.

title: Engineering Assessment and Model Limits
learningObjectives: Explain how to judge acceptability and identify excluded checks.
student: If an allowable normal stress were supplied, explain how you would assess the arm and recommend one modification if it were inadequate. Identify important checks omitted from the base model.
instructor:
{{seat_assessment}}

A complete design must also evaluate attachment and weld stresses, local tube-wall behavior, stress concentrations, fatigue, impact and dynamic occupant loads, stiffness and deflection, connection flexibility, manufacturing quality, and applicable machinery and seating safety requirements.
